A_target.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Topological Space|topological space]] and $x \in X$.
Then the [[Definition:Homotopy Group|homotopy group]] $\map {\pi_n} {X, x}$ is a [[Definition:Group|group]] for $n \ge 1$, [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian]] for $n \ge 2$, and [[Definition:Functor|functorial]] in based maps.

B_source.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Topological Space|topological space]] and $x \in X$.
The [[Definition:Fundamental Group|fundamental group]] $\map {\pi_1} {X, x}$ is the set of [[Definition:Homotopy Class|homotopy classes]] of loops at $x$ under concatenation, and is in general not abelian.

substitutions.the loop, a map from the circle: a map from the n-sphere, or from the n-cube with boundary collapsed
substitutions.concatenation in the single available di: concatenation in any one of n independent directions

derived.the group structure from concatenation: the same, using any one coordinate direction
derived.commutativity for degree at least two: the Eckmann-Hilton argument, using two independent directions

object_map.reformulation: Raise the dimension of the parametrizing cube, which supplies additional independent concatenation directions.

validity_conditions: The case of degree one is the fundamental group, so the generalization specializes correctly.
For degree at least two there are two independent concatenation directions that commute with each other, and the Eckmann-Hilton argument forces the operation to be abelian.
This is why degree one is genuinely exceptional: with only one direction available the argument cannot run, and the fundamental group can be nonabelian.
proof_plan: Replace loops by maps $f: \closedint 0 1^n \to X$ sending the boundary $\partial \closedint 0 1^n$ to $x$.

Define the group operation by concatenation in the $i$th coordinate:
:$\map {\paren {f +_i g} } {t_1, \ldots, t_n} = \begin {cases} \map f {t_1, \ldots, 2 t_i, \ldots, t_n} & : t_i \le \frac 1 2 \\ \map g {t_1, \ldots, 2 t_i - 1, \ldots, t_n} & : t_i \ge \frac 1 2 \end {cases}$

The operations $+_i$ and $+_j$ satisfy the interchange law:
:$\paren {f +_i g} +_j \paren {h +_i k} = \paren {f +_j h} +_i \paren {g +_j k}$
and share the constant map as identity.

For $n \ge 2$ choose $i \ne j$.
By the [[Eckmann-Hilton Argument]], $+_i = +_j$ on homotopy classes and both are [[Definition:Commutative Operation|commutative]].
Hence $\map {\pi_n} {X, x}$ is [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian]] for $n \ge 2$.
{{qed}}
